title: 6 Underused Sends for Behavior-Led Engagement Strategies
summary: These six triggers use external or less commonly tracked signals to identify a relevant moment for re-engagement.
body_markdown:
[Mobile app retention strategies](https://onesignal.com/blog/the-best-retention-strategy-for-you-based-on-your-actual-marketing-role/) can use more than inactivity or broken-streak events. The six triggers below use external or less commonly tracked signals to identify a relevant moment for re-engagement, then send a message tied to the user's likely next action.


### 1. The window before payday, and why it's not just a fintech idea


Most apps that think about payday at all default to messaging the happy moment, the day money lands, and default to fintech as the only category where it matters. Both defaults are worth questioning.


The more overlooked window is often the few days right *before* someone's next payday, when balances are lowest and they're most likely to consider an overdraft, a short-term loan, or a buy-now-pay-later offer they'll regret. A genuinely helpful nudge here (a spend-awareness check-in, a bill heads-up, a suggestion to skip a subscription renewal this cycle)[builds more trust](https://onesignal.com/blog/building-trust-and-driving-revenue-growth-with-fintech-messaging/) than anything sent on payday itself, precisely because most apps ignore this moment or use it to sell something instead of help.


**And the underlying signal isn't fintech-exclusive** . Any app with a purchase or upgrade path,[subscription services](https://onesignal.com/blog/the-best-engagement-loops-for-subscription-apps/) , games with in-app purchases, retail, can use the same idea to time its own messages around a user's likely cash position: a subscription service holding an upgrade offer until just after someone's paid, or a budgeting app choosing to check in right before they're tight on money. None of this requires deep financial data. A single onboarding question ("how often do you get paid?") or a lightweight inferred pattern is enough to tag a user's own cycle and time the message, help or offer, to when it will actually land.


### 2. The device or OS a user just upgraded to


Use device and OS-version data to segment users after an upgrade and send a[mobile push notification](https://onesignal.com/mobile-push) about a feature their current device and app implementation supports. For example, invite eligible users to enable a richer notification format or[Live Activities](https://onesignal.com/blog/best-examples-of-apps-using-live-activities-to-enrich-their-ux/) where available. Include a[deep link](https://onesignal.com/blog/deep-linking-best-practices/) to the relevant setting or feature, and measure whether the message leads to activation or return use. This approach turns an OS upgrade into a timely retention touchpoint while keeping platform support and notification settings specific to each user.


### 3. A support ticket followed by silence


A recent support contact followed by a drop in app opens can identify users who need follow-up. Send the support-contact event from the support system to OneSignal, **then build an audience of users who go quiet afterward** . An automated journey can send a careful push notification or in-app message to that at-risk audience, separate from a general win-back campaign.


### 4. Rewarding a referral when the referred person actually does something, not when they sign up


Set the referral reward to trigger after the referred user completes an activation event, such as finishing onboarding or making a first purchase. Store a tag that links the referrer and referred user, then use the activation event to send the referrer’s acknowledgment or reward. This ties referral incentives to behavior that signals early retention and lets the program measure whether referred users activate.


### 5. Someone who opted back in after opting out


A user who disables push, then re-enables it weeks or months later, is a meaningfully different person than someone opting in for the first time. They had a reason to leave and a reason to come back, and almost every app sends them the identical "welcome" message it sends brand-new users. **Segmenting specifically for re-opt-ins and acknowledging the gap directly** ("good to have notifications back on") is a small copy change sitting on subscription-state data most teams already have and never use for this.


### 6. Contextual relevance from something outside your app entirely


Weather data can trigger relevant mobile push notifications: a coffee app can promote a hot drink when temperatures drop in a user's location, while a fitness app can suggest an indoor routine when rain is forecast. Send weather data from an external API through an integration or[webhook](https://onesignal.com/blog/six-ways-to-use-webhooks-in-journeys/) , then use it to update audience tags and segments. An[automated Journey](https://onesignal.com/journeys) can deliver the message to that audience and measure whether it drives the intended action. This approach uses a timely external signal to make each message relevant to the recipient's conditions.


### Why these are the ones that get missed


These triggers depend on signals beyond in-app activity, such as device status, support events, referral activity, subscription history, or external data. Teams often build lifecycle campaigns around in-app behavior alone, so these opportunities go unnoticed.


Use tags and segmentation to define the audience, connect external systems through integrations, then use an automated journey to send the message and measure the resulting activation, retention, or referral conversion.


None of this requires an enterprise budget, either. Even the best push notification software for small businesses can support every trigger above, since the bottleneck isn't scale, it's noticing the signal exists in the first place.
